title: Facade and Flyweight
scopeHtml: Scope: Facade over subsystems, Flyweight intrinsic/extrinsic state, before/after refactors, when not to use, MediaPlayer, Integer cache, Glide pools.

notes.title: Facade: the idea
notes.html:
A Facade gives one simple front door to a complicated subsystem. Clients call one easy method; the facade orchestrates the many classes behind it. It does not stop you using the subsystem directly if you really need to.

Mechanism: a class that holds references to several subsystem objects and exposes a few coarse-grained methods that call them in the right order.

+----------+      +------------------+       +--------------+
| Client   | ---> | OrderFacade      | ----> | Inventory    |
+----------+      | + placeOrder()   | ----> | Payment      |
                  +------------------+ ----> | Shipping     |
                                       ----> | Notification |

Worked example. Placing an order needs: reserve stock (1 call), charge card (1 call), create shipment (1 call), send email (1 call). Without a facade each of 12 screens repeats those 4 calls and their error handling: 48 call sites. With a facade there are 4 calls in 1 place plus 12 one-line callers.

Industry examples. Android MediaPlayer hides decoders, buffers and audio output behind start()/pause(). Retrofit's Retrofit.create() front door. SLF4J LoggerFactory. Spring's JdbcTemplate is a facade over JDBC connection, statement, result set and cleanup. Stripe's PaymentIntent API is a facade over card networks, 3DS and fraud checks.

Everyday analogy. A hotel concierge: you say "dinner for two at 8" and they handle the phone calls, booking and the taxi.

Decision gravity. Easy to add and reversible; the facade's method signatures become a public contract. Moving a transaction boundary inside it later (all-or-nothing vs best-effort) is behavior-changing, so decide consistency rules up front.

Common interview traps.

  • Facade vs Adapter: Facade simplifies MANY classes into a new simple interface; Adapter converts ONE interface into an existing expected one.
  • Letting the facade become a god class holding all business logic.

notes.title: Facade in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before.

// BEFORE: every caller knows the order and the failure handling
inventory.reserve(sku, qty);
try {
    payment.charge(card, amount);
} catch (PaymentException e) {
    inventory.release(sku, qty);   // easy to forget
    throw e;
}
shipping.create(address, sku);
email.send(user, "Order placed");

After.

class OrderFacade {
    private final Inventory inventory; private final Payment payment;
    private final Shipping shipping;   private final Notifier notifier;
    OrderFacade(Inventory i, Payment p, Shipping s, Notifier n) {
        inventory = i; payment = p; shipping = s; notifier = n;
    }
    public void placeOrder(String user, String sku, int qty, double amount) {
        inventory.reserve(sku, qty);
        try {
            payment.charge(user, amount);
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            inventory.release(sku, qty);   // compensation lives in one place
            throw e;
        }
        shipping.create(user, sku);
        notifier.send(user, "Order placed");
    }
}
// facade.placeOrder("anu", "SKU-9", 2, 998.0);
class OrderFacade(
    private val inventory: Inventory, private val payment: Payment,
    private val shipping: Shipping, private val notifier: Notifier,
) {
    fun placeOrder(user: String, sku: String, qty: Int, amount: Double) {
        inventory.reserve(sku, qty)
        runCatching { payment.charge(user, amount) }
            .onFailure { inventory.release(sku, qty); throw it }
        shipping.create(user, sku)
        notifier.send(user, "Order placed")
    }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the failure path (compensation) which is the real value of the facade.
  • Hiding the subsystem entirely so power users cannot reach it.

notes.title: Facade: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not use it when the subsystem is already one simple class; wrapping it adds a pointless layer. Do not use it to hide a bad design you could fix.

Avoid it if it grows to 40 methods: that is a god object; split by use case (OrderFacade, RefundFacade).

Distributed variant: a facade across microservices (an API gateway or BFF, backend-for-frontend) adds latency (+1 hop, often 1 to 5 ms) and becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure unless replicated.

Worked example. A AppFacade with 60 methods meant every release touched it and merge conflicts hit weekly. Splitting into 5 focused facades cut conflicts to rare.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling any service class a facade. A facade specifically simplifies a complex subsystem.
  • Not thinking about transactions when the facade crosses services.

notes.title: Flyweight: the idea
notes.html:
Flyweight saves memory by sharing the common, unchanging part of many similar objects. Split object state into intrinsic (shared, immutable, stored in the flyweight) and extrinsic (varies per use, passed in by the caller).

Mechanism: a factory keeps a pool (map). When asked for a flyweight with a given intrinsic key, it returns the existing one or creates it once.

 Context objects (millions)           Flyweight pool (few)
+-------------------------+          +----------------------+
| Tree: x=10, y=7, kind --+--------->| TreeType "Oak"       |
| Tree: x=44, y=2, kind --+--------->|  texture (2 MB)      |
| Tree: x=91, y=30,kind --+--------->|  mesh                |
+-------------------------+          +----------------------+
 extrinsic: x, y                      intrinsic: texture, mesh

Worked example. A game draws 1,000,000 trees of 5 species. A texture and mesh is 2 MB. Naively: 1,000,000 x 2 MB = 2 TB (impossible). With Flyweight: 5 x 2 MB = 10 MB shared, plus 1,000,000 x 16 bytes (x, y, type reference) = 16 MB. About 26 MB total.

Industry examples. Integer.valueOf(n) caches -128 to 127; so Integer a = 100, b = 100; a == b is true but with 1000 it is false. String interning (the string pool). Android Glide and Fresco bitmap pools, Pools.SimplePool and RecyclerView's shared RecycledViewPool (reuse of view holders). Text editors share one glyph object per character.

Everyday analogy. A print shop keeps one metal stamp per letter and presses it at different positions, instead of carving a new stamp for every letter on the page.

Decision gravity. An optimization: reversible but invasive, because you split state into intrinsic and extrinsic everywhere. Do it only after measuring memory. It trades memory for a little CPU and API awkwardness.

Common interview traps.

  • Flyweight objects MUST be immutable (or at least their intrinsic part); otherwise one change corrupts all users.
  • Using == on boxed Integers is a classic bug that stems from the flyweight cache.

notes.title: Flyweight in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before.

// BEFORE: each Tree owns its own 2 MB texture copy
class Tree {
    final byte[] texture = loadTexture("oak.png"); // 2 MB each
    int x, y;
}

After.

import java.util.*;

final class TreeType {                    // flyweight: immutable, shared
    final String name; final byte[] texture;
    TreeType(String name) { this.name = name; this.texture = new byte[2 * 1024 * 1024]; }
}

final class TreeTypeFactory {
    private static final Map<String, TreeType> POOL = new HashMap<>();
    static TreeType get(String name) {
        return POOL.computeIfAbsent(name, TreeType::new);   // not thread-safe pool = see note
    }
}

class Tree {                              // context: only extrinsic state
    final int x, y; final TreeType type;
    Tree(int x, int y, TreeType type) { this.x = x; this.y = y; this.type = type; }
}

// new Tree(10, 7, TreeTypeFactory.get("Oak"))  -> same TreeType for all oaks
class TreeType(val name: String) { val texture = ByteArray(2 * 1024 * 1024) }

object TreeTypeFactory {
    private val pool = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, TreeType>()
    fun get(name: String) = pool.computeIfAbsent(name) { TreeType(it) }
}

class Tree(val x: Int, val y: Int, val type: TreeType)

Thread safety. A plain HashMap pool breaks under concurrent access; use ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent (Kotlin version above). Also the pool can leak if keys are unbounded; consider WeakReference values or an LRU.

Common interview traps.

  • Sharing mutable state in the "flyweight".
  • Forgetting the factory; without it nothing is shared.
  • Not stating the numbers (2 TB vs 26 MB) that justify the pattern.

notes.title: Flyweight: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not use it when there are few objects (a thousand small objects cost kilobytes) or when little state is shareable. The pattern then only adds complexity.

Do not use it when objects are mutable per instance or when extrinsic state is costly to compute or pass on every call (CPU cost beats memory savings).

On modern JVMs and Android, premature pooling can hurt: young-generation GC is cheap, and object pools add contention, stale state bugs and memory that never gets freed. Pool large or expensive things (bitmaps, DB connections), not small ones.

Worked example. A team pooled 24-byte Point objects. The pool lock added about 40 ns per access, more than the allocation it saved (about 10 ns), and the heap dropped by 0 MB. They removed it.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming Flyweight always speeds things up. It saves memory, often at CPU cost.
  • Confusing it with caching: caching avoids recomputation; Flyweight shares identical immutable objects.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Facade: a simple front door over a complex subsystem; put orchestration and compensation in one place; keep the subsystem accessible; do not grow a god facade. Examples: MediaPlayer, JdbcTemplate, Stripe PaymentIntent, BFF/API gateway.
  • Facade simplifies many classes; Adapter converts one interface.
  • Flyweight: share immutable intrinsic state through a factory; pass extrinsic state in. Example numbers: 2 TB down to 26 MB. Examples: Integer.valueOf cache, string pool, Glide bitmap pool, RecycledViewPool.
  • Make flyweights immutable and thread-safe; avoid pooling small objects on modern GCs.
  • Use Flyweight only after measuring; use Facade when callers repeat the same multi-step recipe.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Facade pattern? Give a real example and say what it does not do.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks that you see a facade as a simplifier of a subsystem, not a wall around it and not a dumping ground.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Facade gives one simple entry point to a complicated subsystem. The client calls placeOrder(...); the facade calls inventory, payment, shipping and notification in the right order, with the failure handling. It does not remove the subsystem: power users can still reach the parts. Android MediaPlayer and Spring JdbcTemplate are examples.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The facade holds references to several subsystem classes and exposes a few coarse-grained methods. The value is not fewer lines, it is that the recipe, ordering and compensation live in one place. Twelve screens that each repeated four calls are 48 call sites; with a facade it is 4 calls once plus 12 one-liners.

Client -> OrderFacade.placeOrder() -> Inventory.reserve
                                   -> Payment.charge (on failure: Inventory.release)
                                   -> Shipping.create
                                   -> Notifier.send

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

class OrderFacade {
    private final Inventory inv; private final Payment pay; private final Shipping ship; private final Notifier n;
    OrderFacade(Inventory i, Payment p, Shipping s, Notifier n) { inv = i; pay = p; ship = s; this.n = n; }
    void placeOrder(String user, String sku, int qty, double amount) {
        inv.reserve(sku, qty);
        try { pay.charge(user, amount); } catch (RuntimeException e) { inv.release(sku, qty); throw e; }
        ship.create(user, sku);
        n.send(user, "Order placed");
    }
}
class OrderFacade(private val inv: Inventory, private val pay: Payment, private val ship: Shipping, private val n: Notifier) {
    fun placeOrder(user: String, sku: String, qty: Int, amount: Double) {
        inv.reserve(sku, qty)
        try { pay.charge(user, amount) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { inv.release(sku, qty); throw e }
        ship.create(user, sku); n.send(user, "Order placed")
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Letting the facade become a god class holding business logic.
  • Forgetting the failure path, which is the real value.
  • Hiding the subsystem so power users have no access.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Facade vs Adapter? -> Facade simplifies many classes with a new interface; Adapter fits one class to an existing interface.
  2. Is Service just a facade? -> Not automatically; a facade specifically hides a complex subsystem.
  3. What about transactions? -> Decide all-or-nothing vs best-effort up front; it becomes a public contract.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "simple interface to complex system". Senior points at compensation and consistency rules living there and says the subsystem stays reachable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout recipe copied across 12 screens had a forgotten release() in 3 of them; stock leaked until a nightly job fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing service compares quantities. In tests, orders of quantity 100 match; in production an order of quantity 1,000 never matches its limit and is rejected.

Integer limit = Integer.valueOf(1000);
Integer qty = order.getQuantity();       // returns Integer 1000
if (qty == limit) { approve(order); }    // never true for 1000, true for 100
questions.promptHtml: Why does this behave differently for 100 and 1,000, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Java is inconsistent" or "use equals for strings but == is fine for numbers".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are these boxed Integer or int? Where is the value created: autoboxing, valueOf, deserialization?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the comparison to equals or unbox.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) == on boxed Integers compares references, and Integer.valueOf caches only -128..127; (b) a different type (Long vs Integer); (c) data mismatch.
  4. How I'd verify each: Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b is true, 1000, 1000 is false (default cache upper bound; configurable on HotSpot via -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax, verify for your JVM).
  5. Root cause: Integer.valueOf is a Flyweight: it returns shared instances for small values, so == accidentally works for them. Above the range each call allocates a new object.
  6. Fix: qty.equals(limit) or compare as primitives qty.intValue() == limit. In Kotlin use == (it calls equals), not ===.
  7. Prevention: static analysis rule against == on wrapper types (Error Prone, IDE inspection); tests with values beyond 127.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise the cache bound as a fix: it hides the bug and wastes memory.
if (qty.equals(limit)) approve(order);
if (qty == limit) approve(order)          // Kotlin == is equals, safe
// qty === limit would repeat the Java bug

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does Long have the same trap? -> Long.valueOf caches -128..127 as well.
  • Does a String compare with == fail similarly? -> Literals are interned (pool) so it sometimes works; runtime strings are new objects.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a limits check passed all tests with small data and failed for the first large customer, whose quantity exceeded 127.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Java.
  • Hire: explains the cache range and uses equals.
  • Strong hire: ties it to Flyweight, adds a lint rule and a boundary test.

questions.promptHtml: A teammate says "our PaymentService is an adapter". Another says "no, a facade". How do you decide which pattern a wrapper is, and does it matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests intent-based reasoning about structural patterns and whether you can say why naming matters.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I ask two things: how many classes does it wrap, and who defined the interface it exposes? Adapter converts one existing interface into the one the client already expects. Facade invents a new simpler interface over several classes. A wrapper over one vendor SDK that implements my PaymentGateway is an Adapter; OrderFacade over inventory, payment and shipping is a Facade.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Naming matters because each pattern carries rules. An adapter is logic-free translation and replaceable per vendor; a facade owns orchestration and failure policy. A class doing both is a smell: split into adapters per vendor, called by a facade. In a notification service the layering is NotificationFacade -> decorators -> TwilioAdapter -> SDK.

Adapter: Client -> Target (given) -> Adapter -> 1 Adaptee
Facade : Client -> NewSimpleAPI   -> Facade  -> N classes

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

class TwilioAdapter implements Sender { public boolean send(String u, String t) { return sdk.sendSms(u, t, false) == 200; } }
class NotificationFacade { private final Sender s; NotificationFacade(Sender s) { this.s = s; } boolean notify(String u, String t) { return s.send(u, t); } }
class TwilioAdapter(private val sdk: TwilioSdk) : Sender { override fun send(user: String, text: String) = sdk.sendSms(user, text, false) == 200 }
class NotificationFacade(private val s: Sender) { fun notify(user: String, text: String) = s.send(user, text) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling any wrapper "a facade".
  • A facade that merely renames one method of one class (an adapter without a target).
  • Mixing orchestration into an adapter.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a facade use adapters? -> Yes, one per vendor SDK behind it.
  2. Can an adapter wrap many classes? -> It can, but then it is orchestrating and is probably a facade.
  3. Does it matter in code review? -> Yes: it tells reviewers what belongs there (translation only vs coordination).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives one-line definitions. Senior uses the two-question test and shows how they layer.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An "adapter" that also retried, validated and logged hid a double-charge bug because no one knew it did orchestration.

questions.contextHtml:
Twelve screens place orders with this recipe copy-pasted. Support finds that stock is "reserved forever" for some failed payments (about 0.4% of orders, 600 units stuck this month). One screen sends the email before shipping.

inventory.reserve(sku, qty);
payment.charge(card, amount);       // can throw PaymentException
shipping.create(address, sku);
email.send(user, "Order placed");
questions.promptHtml: Refactor it and show how you would unit test the new class.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Wraps the four calls in a static OrderUtil.place(...) with no failure handling and no way to inject fakes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What should happen if shipping fails after charging: refund or retry? Is email best-effort? Is this one DB or several services?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run a script that releases reservations older than N minutes that have no successful payment.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing compensation on PaymentException in some copies; copies diverged on order.
  4. How I'd verify each: Diff the 12 call sites; query reservations with no payment older than 15 minutes.
  5. Root cause: The recipe and its failure policy are duplicated, so each copy has its own bugs.
  6. Fix: OrderFacade with injected collaborators; reserve first, charge in try/catch with release on failure, refund on shipping failure, email last and best-effort. Screens call placeOrder only.
  7. Prevention: tests on the facade with fakes for each failure point; a lint rule that screens do not import Inventory directly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The facade does not become a transaction manager across services; for real consistency use a saga or outbox. I would not hide the subsystem so support tools can still call it.
class OrderFacadeTest {
    void releasesStockWhenPaymentFails() {
        FakeInventory inv = new FakeInventory();
        OrderFacade f = new OrderFacade(inv, (u, a) -> { throw new RuntimeException("declined"); }, shipping, notifier);
        try { f.placeOrder("u", "SKU", 2, 100); } catch (RuntimeException ignored) { }
        assert inv.reserved("SKU") == 0;
    }
}
@Test fun releasesStockWhenPaymentFails() {
    val inv = FakeInventory()
    val f = OrderFacade(inv, { _, _ -> error("declined") }, shipping, notifier)
    runCatching { f.placeOrder("u", "SKU", 2, 100.0) }
    check(inv.reserved("SKU") == 0)
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Payment times out but succeeded. -> Use idempotency keys and reconcile, never release stock blindly.
  • Email provider down. -> Best-effort: enqueue and retry; do not fail the order.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: stock leaked quietly from forgotten compensations in a few copied screens; a facade plus a reconciliation job closed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: static helper without failure handling.
  • Hire: facade with compensation and injected dependencies.
  • Strong hire: states failure policy per step, tests failure points, mentions idempotency and saga.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the Flyweight pattern. What are intrinsic and extrinsic state, and why must a flyweight be immutable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you can separate shareable state from context state and reason about sharing hazards.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Flyweight saves memory by sharing the common, unchanging part of many similar objects. Intrinsic state is shared and stored in the flyweight, for example a tree's texture and mesh; extrinsic state varies per use and is passed in or held by the context, such as x and y. A factory returns one flyweight per key. It must be immutable because a change to a shared object changes it for every user.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A million trees of 5 species, with 2 MB textures: 2 TB naively; with Flyweight 5 x 2 MB = 10 MB plus 1,000,000 contexts of about 16 bytes (x, y, reference) = 16 MB, so about 26 MB. Without the factory nothing is shared. JDK examples: Integer.valueOf cache, string pool, RecycledViewPool, Glide bitmap pools.

Tree(x,y,type) x 1,000,000 --> TreeType "Oak" (texture) x 5

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

final class TreeType { final String name; final byte[] texture; TreeType(String n) { name = n; texture = new byte[2 << 20]; } }
class Tree { final int x, y; final TreeType type; Tree(int x, int y, TreeType t) { this.x = x; this.y = y; type = t; } }
class TreeType(val name: String) { val texture = ByteArray(2 shl 20) }
class Tree(val x: Int, val y: Int, val type: TreeType)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mutable "flyweights" shared by all contexts.
  • No factory, so no sharing.
  • Calling it caching: Flyweight shares identical immutable objects; caching avoids recomputation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Integer a = 1000, b = 1000; a == b fail? -> Outside the cache range each boxing creates a new object.
  2. What is the cost? -> A factory lookup and extrinsic state passed on each call.
  3. How do you avoid a leaking pool? -> Bound it with an LRU or weak references.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "share objects to save memory". Senior gives the numbers, the immutability requirement, thread safety and when not to pool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A map renderer kept a texture per marker; moving to shared marker types cut memory by 90% and ended OOM crashes.

questions.contextHtml:
A map app shows up to 200,000 markers (pins) at once. Each pin object holds lat, lon, a title, and an Icon object with a 64 KB decoded bitmap. There are 12 distinct icon kinds (restaurant, fuel, ATM...). Memory today:

200,000 pins x (64 KB icon + ~50 B fields) = ~12.8 GB  -> OutOfMemoryError on a 4 GB heap

The icon is never modified after load.
questions.promptHtml: Redesign the model, compute the new memory, and say what you would measure first.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more RAM" or "lazy-load icons per pin", which still allocates one per pin.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the icon truly identical per kind? Is the title per pin? Do icons change with zoom level?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap visible markers by clustering; stop allocating per-pin bitmaps.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the duplicated bitmaps dominate memory; (b) the per-pin object overhead (header 12-16 B plus fields, titles) is small by comparison.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump (for example Android Studio profiler or a JVM heap dump) and check retained size by class; expect Bitmap/byte[] to be nearly all of it.
  5. Root cause: Intrinsic state (the icon) is stored per instance.
  6. Fix: Flyweight IconType per kind from a factory; Pin(lat, lon, title, iconType) keeps only extrinsic state. New memory: 12 x 64 KB = 768 KB for icons plus 200,000 x about 50 B = 10 MB, so about 11 MB instead of 12.8 GB.
  7. Prevention: a memory test with 200k pins and a heap budget; review rule that bitmaps come only from the icon factory.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not pool the small Pin objects. Flyweights are immutable, so a "highlight" must be an extrinsic flag, not a mutation of the shared icon.
final class IconType { final String kind; final byte[] bitmap; IconType(String k) { kind = k; bitmap = load(k); } }
final class IconFactory {
    private static final Map<String, IconType> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    static IconType get(String kind) { return POOL.computeIfAbsent(kind, IconType::new); }
}
record Pin(double lat, double lon, String title, IconType icon, boolean highlighted) { }
class IconType(val kind: String) { val bitmap = load(kind) }
object IconFactory {
    private val pool = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, IconType>()
    fun get(kind: String) = pool.computeIfAbsent(kind) { IconType(it) }
}
data class Pin(val lat: Double, val lon: Double, val title: String, val icon: IconType, val highlighted: Boolean = false)

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Icons vary by zoom level. -> Key the pool by (kind, zoomBucket); the pool stays small.
  • Users can upload custom icons. -> Unbounded keys; use an LRU with weak values.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a mapping client had each marker decode its own icon; sharing one decoded bitmap per kind turned a crash on dense city views into a 40 MB footprint.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more RAM.
  • Hire: shared icon via factory with correct memory math.
  • Strong hire: profiles first, keeps highlight extrinsic, bounds the pool.

questions.contextHtml:
A text renderer shares one Glyph flyweight per character through a factory. Under a 32-thread export job the process occasionally hangs at 100% CPU, and sometimes two different Glyph objects exist for the same character (heap dump shows 3 instances of Glyph('e')).

final class GlyphFactory {
    private static final Map<Character, Glyph> POOL = new HashMap<>();
    static Glyph get(char c) {
        Glyph g = POOL.get(c);
        if (g == null) { g = new Glyph(c); POOL.put(c, g); }   // loads a 40 KB shape
        return g;
    }
}
jstack: 6 threads RUNNABLE at java.util.HashMap.getNode / HashMap.put (resize)
questions.promptHtml: Explain both symptoms and fix them without losing the sharing.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make get synchronized." Correct but a global lock on the hot path, and it ignores the loading cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the pool pre-populated for known characters? How expensive is new Glyph? Is the key set bounded?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Switch to ConcurrentHashMap and computeIfAbsent right away.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) unsynchronized HashMap under concurrent put and resize corrupts the table (busy loops were a known failure mode in older JDKs; the stack shows threads in HashMap); (b) check-then-act race creating duplicate flyweights.
  4. How I'd verify each: A stress test with 32 threads calling get('e') and asserting identity; the jstack frames confirm unsynchronized map access.
  5. Root cause: A non-thread-safe map used as a shared pool with a check-then-put sequence.
  6. Fix: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent(c, Glyph::new): atomic per key, so one instance per key. Keep the mapping function short, because computeIfAbsent blocks other updates on the same bin while it runs (and must not touch the same map recursively).
  7. Prevention: a concurrency test in CI asserting == identity across threads; immutability of Glyph.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use double-checked locking by hand when the JDK gives it. If loading is slow, pre-populate the pool at startup (the key set is small) so the hot path is read-only.
final class GlyphFactory {
    private static final ConcurrentHashMap<Character, Glyph> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    static Glyph get(char c) { return POOL.computeIfAbsent(c, Glyph::new); }
}
object GlyphFactory {
    private val pool = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<Char, Glyph>()
    fun get(c: Char): Glyph = pool.computeIfAbsent(c) { Glyph(it) }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not a plain synchronized? -> It works, but every glyph lookup contends on one lock.
  • The key space is the whole of Unicode. -> Bound it with an LRU or weak values; unbounded pools leak.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a shared lookup table built lazily by many threads produced duplicate objects and rare hangs only during large exports, never in tests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the CPU or the JVM.
  • Hire: finds the unsynchronized map and uses computeIfAbsent.
  • Strong hire: explains both symptoms, notes computeIfAbsent pitfalls, pre-populates and bounds the pool.

questions.contextHtml:
AppFacade started as a clean entry point. It now has 60 methods across orders, refunds, users, reports and admin tools, 3,800 lines, and is injected into the web app, the mobile API and the admin panel. Last quarter, 41 of 55 merged PRs touched it, with weekly merge conflicts. A refund change broke a report method because both share a private cache field.

git log --since=3.months -- AppFacade.java | grep -c commit   -> 41
questions.promptHtml: How do you break it up safely, and what design rule stops it growing back?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Mechanically splits files alphabetically, keeps the shared state and adds a new super-facade over the pieces.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which methods change together (from git history)? Who calls which methods? Is there shared state or a transaction spanning methods?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze additions; any new method needs a new focused facade.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) multiple use cases share one class; (b) shared private state couples unrelated flows; (c) callers want different subsets.
  4. How I'd verify each: Co-change analysis from history, call-graph per client, inspect fields used by each method group.
  5. Root cause: A facade is a simplifier per use case; this one became a service locator for the whole app.
  6. Fix: Split by use case: OrderFacade, RefundFacade, ReportFacade, AdminFacade, each with the collaborators it needs and no shared mutable state. Move the cache into its own component injected where needed. Migrate callers one at a time, leaving AppFacade delegating and marked deprecated, then delete it.
  7. Prevention: a size limit (for example 10 public methods) in review and an architecture test that facades do not depend on each other.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do a big-bang rewrite. Strangler-style delegation keeps every release shippable; the cost is a few weeks of duplicate entry points.
@Deprecated
class AppFacade {
    private final OrderFacade orders; private final RefundFacade refunds;
    AppFacade(OrderFacade o, RefundFacade r) { orders = o; refunds = r; }
    void placeOrder(OrderRequest r) { orders.placeOrder(r); }       // delegate while callers migrate
    void refund(String id) { refunds.refund(id); }
}
@Deprecated("use OrderFacade / RefundFacade")
class AppFacade(private val orders: OrderFacade, private val refunds: RefundFacade) {
    fun placeOrder(r: OrderRequest) = orders.placeOrder(r)
    fun refund(id: String) = refunds.refund(id)
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mobile wants one call that does order and notification. -> A BFF endpoint or a thin screen-specific facade over the two, not a method in the god class.
  • Is a Facade ever allowed to be big? -> Only if it is one cohesive use case; size is a smell signal, not a rule.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a 60-method facade caused weekly conflicts; five focused facades dropped conflicts to a handful per quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: alphabetical split.
  • Hire: splits by use case and removes shared state.
  • Strong hire: incremental strangler migration, size rule, architecture test.

questions.contextHtml:
A game shows 5,000 enemies of type "Goblin" sharing one EnemyType flyweight. A designer adds a feature "frozen enemies turn blue". After a freeze spell on one goblin, every goblin on screen turns blue, and QA files "freeze spell affects all enemies".

final class EnemyType { String name; Color color; Sprite sprite; }   // shared per kind
class Enemy {
    final EnemyType type; int x, y;
    void freeze() { type.color = Color.BLUE; }
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does this happen, and how do you model frozen state correctly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clone the EnemyType for the frozen goblin", defeating the sharing, or setting the color back with a timer.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which state is per enemy (hp, frozen, position)? Is the tint rendering-only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the freeze visual; the logic can stay.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) mutation of shared intrinsic state; (b) duplicate instances (no, QA sees all enemies change, so one shared object).
  4. How I'd verify each: Print System.identityHashCode(type) across enemies: identical.
  5. Root cause: Per-instance state was written into a shared flyweight.
  6. Fix: Make EnemyType final with final fields (immutable). Put frozen in Enemy (extrinsic state) and pass a tint to the renderer: renderer.draw(type.sprite, x, y, frozen ? BLUE : type.color).
  7. Prevention: declare flyweights as immutable (final fields, records); a test that type fields are final via reflection or review rule.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not clone per enemy; that loses the memory savings (5,000 sprites instead of 1).
record EnemyType(String name, Color color, Sprite sprite) { }       // immutable flyweight
class Enemy {
    final EnemyType type; int x, y; boolean frozen;
    void freeze() { frozen = true; }
    Color tint() { return frozen ? Color.BLUE : type.color(); }
}
data class EnemyType(val name: String, val color: Color, val sprite: Sprite)   // immutable
class Enemy(val type: EnemyType, var x: Int, var y: Int) {
    var frozen = false
    fun tint() = if (frozen) Color.BLUE else type.color
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A "buff all goblins" spell is wanted. -> Then it really is shared state; create a new EnemyType version and switch references, or keep a global modifier object.
  • Thread safety? -> Immutable flyweights are safe to share across threads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a theme object shared across screens was mutated by one dialog and recolored the whole app until restart.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: clones the type.
  • Hire: finds the shared mutation and moves state to the enemy.
  • Strong hire: makes the flyweight immutable by construction and keeps the renderer tint extrinsic.

questions.contextHtml:
To "reduce GC" on an Android feed, a teammate pooled Point(x, y) objects (24 bytes each) behind a synchronized PointPool. Frame stats after the change:

before: alloc 18 MB/s, GC pauses avg 2 ms, jank frames 1.1%
after : alloc 17 MB/s, GC pauses avg 2 ms, jank frames 2.9%, PointPool.acquire avg 40 ns (lock contention)

Allocation of a small object costs about 10 ns on the same device. The pool also has a bug where a point released twice is handed to two callers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Pooling reduces garbage, so it is good; fix the double release." It ignores the measured results.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What was the GC problem that motivated this? Was it measured (allocation profile)? Which thread acquires points?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert; it made jank worse and added a double-hand-out bug.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the allocation was not the bottleneck; (b) lock contention costs more than allocation; (c) objects retained by the pool survive into older generations and add GC work.
  4. How I'd verify each: Allocation tracker or profiler for the real source of the 18 MB/s; compare jank via frame metrics; contention in a trace.
  5. Root cause: Applying Flyweight/pooling to tiny, short-lived objects on a generational GC where allocation is cheap.
  6. Fix: Revert. If garbage truly matters, find the big allocators (bitmaps, lists in onDraw) and fix those: reuse a single scratch object or pass primitives.
  7. Prevention: require before/after numbers for any pool; reviewer checklist: "what did the profile say?".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would pool large or expensive things (bitmaps, DB connections, thread-local buffers) after measuring, not 24-byte values.
// Instead of pooling: avoid the allocation in the hot loop
void onDraw(Canvas c) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) c.drawCircle(xs[i], ys[i], r, paint);   // primitive arrays, no Point objects
}
override fun onDraw(c: Canvas) {
    for (i in 0 until n) c.drawCircle(xs[i], ys[i], r, paint)
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pool is lock-free? -> Contention drops but stale-state and leak bugs remain; the benefit is still not proven.
  • When is pooling right? -> Expensive creation (bitmaps, connections, parsers) with a measured win.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a pool of tiny objects was removed after profiling showed the lock cost more than the allocation it avoided and the heap did not shrink.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the pool.
  • Hire: reads the numbers and reverts.
  • Strong hire: locates the real allocator, states when pooling pays and requires profiling in review.

questions.contextHtml:
The monolith OrderFacade calls 4 modules in-process in one DB transaction. You are splitting inventory, payment and shipping into services over a quarter, with live traffic at about 300 orders/min. A partial run showed:

reserve OK -> charge OK -> shipping HTTP timeout (3 s) -> facade throws -> client retries
result: customer charged twice on retry, stock reserved twice for 37 orders
questions.promptHtml: What changes in the facade, and how do you migrate without losing consistency?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in @Transactional." That cannot span HTTP calls to other services.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What consistency does the business need (refund on failure vs eventual)? Are the new services idempotent? Which step can be asynchronous?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add an order id as an idempotency key to every downstream call; stop client-side blind retries.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the timeout turned an unknown outcome into a failure; (b) calls are not idempotent; (c) no compensation.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace by order id; find orders with more than one payment record; check how shipping handled the repeated request.
  5. Root cause: The monolith's atomic transaction was silently lost when steps became network calls; the facade still pretends to be all-or-nothing.
  6. Fix: Turn the facade into an orchestrator (saga): persist order state (RESERVED, PAID, SHIPPED), each step idempotent with the order id as key, explicit compensations (release, refund), and shipping moved to an async queue with retries. The client gets "accepted" and polls or receives an event.
  7. Prevention: chaos tests that kill or delay each service; reconciliation job for orders in intermediate states.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use distributed two-phase commit across services for this. The cost is eventual consistency and explicit states; the gain is availability.
void placeOrder(Order o) {
    state.save(o.id(), RESERVED);  inventory.reserve(o.id(), o.sku(), o.qty());      // idempotent by id
    try { payment.charge(o.id(), o.amount()); state.save(o.id(), PAID); }
    catch (RuntimeException e) { inventory.release(o.id()); state.save(o.id(), FAILED); throw e; }
    shippingQueue.publish(new CreateShipment(o.id()));                               // async, retried
}
fun placeOrder(o: Order) {
    state.save(o.id, RESERVED); inventory.reserve(o.id, o.sku, o.qty)
    try { payment.charge(o.id, o.amount); state.save(o.id, PAID) }
    catch (e: RuntimeException) { inventory.release(o.id); state.save(o.id, FAILED); throw e }
    shippingQueue.publish(CreateShipment(o.id))
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Payment succeeded but we crashed before saving PAID. -> On restart, retry charge with the same key; the provider returns the first result.
  • Could the facade become a bottleneck? -> It is stateless apart from the store; scale it horizontally.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: after the split, timeouts produced double charges until idempotency keys and a saga state table were added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: relies on a local transaction.
  • Hire: idempotency keys and compensation.
  • Strong hire: saga states, async steps, reconciliation and the reason against 2PC.

questions.promptHtml: How is Flyweight different from a cache and from an object pool, and when does each one apply?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers need to know these three do different jobs and fail in different ways.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Flyweight shares identical immutable objects to save memory. A cache stores computed results to avoid recomputation or I/O and needs invalidation. An object pool reuses mutable, expensive-to-create objects such as connections, handing out one at a time and taking it back. Flyweight is about many users of one object at once; a pool is exclusive use; a cache is about stale versus fresh data.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Flyweight Cache Object pool
Goal memory speed, fewer calls cost of creation
Object state immutable, shared any, may expire mutable, reset on return
Concurrent use many at once many readers one at a time
Main failure mutation corrupts all stale data, stampede leak, double release
Example Integer.valueOf, string pool HTTP cache, @Cacheable DB connection pool

Overlap exists: a glyph factory is flyweight and also memoized; Glide's bitmap pool is a pool, its memory cache is a cache.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Glyph g = GlyphFactory.get('e');                 // flyweight: shared forever
Conn c = pool.acquire(); try { c.run(); } finally { pool.release(c); }   // pool: exclusive then returned
val g = GlyphFactory.get('e')                      // flyweight
pool.acquire().use { it.run() }                    // pool with guaranteed release

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating a mutable object as a flyweight.
  • Pooling small objects and slowing things down.
  • Forgetting release in a pool (leak) or double release.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is String.intern a flyweight? -> Yes, a shared immutable pool, but interning arbitrary strings can bloat it.
  2. Why pool DB connections but not Point? -> Creation costs milliseconds and a server resource; allocation of Point costs nanoseconds.
  3. Which fails with a hot-key expiry? -> A cache (stampede); use per-key locks or coalescing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE blurs them. Senior separates them by sharing mode and state mutability and names each failure mode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team "pooled" mutable parsers without resetting state, so a field from one request leaked into the next response.
